summary: Discusses how QUIC's design and its visible wire image affect network operations involving QUIC traffic. It acts as a user's manual for the wire image, giving guidance to network operators and equipment vendors who rely on transport-aware network functions. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: QUIC hides most of what it does, so people who run networks wonder what they can still see. This explains what is visible and what is not.

questions: what can network operators see in quic traffic
how to manage quic in a network
what is the quic wire image

subtitle: A guide for network operators managing QUIC traffic

tldr.problem: QUIC is a new encrypted transport protocol that hides most of its content from network operators. Operators need guidance on what they can and cannot observe about QUIC traffic to manage networks effectively.
tldr.mechanism: The document examines QUIC's wire image (the visible unencrypted header information) and explains what information is exposed at each stage of a connection, from the handshake through steady-state operation.
tldr.outcome: Network operators understand which QUIC operations are observable on the wire, what management tasks are possible, and where they must cooperate with endpoints because QUIC's encryption prevents in-path modification.

facts.label: Long header packets
facts.value: Used during setup; carry version and connection IDs in the clear

facts.label: Short header packets
facts.value: Used after connection; expose only destination connection ID and spin bit

facts.label: Recommended NAT timeout
facts.value: At least 2 minutes, despite being UDP

facts.label: Minimum QUIC packet size
facts.value: 1200 bytes during handshake, for amplification attack protection

today: RFC 9312 is Informational. It is not a standard but a guide for network operators who must manage QUIC traffic. As QUIC deployment grows and becomes the transport for HTTP/3 and other applications, understanding these management capabilities and constraints is essential for network operations.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 9312 is a user's manual for managing QUIC traffic on networks. QUIC is a modern transport protocol designed to be faster and more efficient than TCP, especially for applications like HTTP/3. Unlike TCP, QUIC encrypts nearly all of its control information, meaning that network devices sitting on the path cannot see or modify most of the protocol's internal workings.

This document guides network operators and equipment vendors who need to manage QUIC traffic. It explains what is visible in QUIC's wire image (the unencrypted parts of the packet headers) and how that information can be used for network operations. It also clarifies where traditional network management practices cannot work with QUIC and where operators need cooperation from the endpoints themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: Network operators are used to watching and controlling TCP traffic. QUIC is different because it hides most of what it does. This explains what you can still see and what you need to do differently.

sections.title: The QUIC Wire Image
sections.content:
QUIC packets have two types of headers: long headers and short headers. The long header is used during connection setup and carries visible information including the version number, source connection ID, and destination connection ID. The short header is used after the connection is established and is much smaller, exposing only the destination connection ID and the spin bit.

The version number identifies which version of QUIC is in use. During handshake, endpoints exchange their versions so observers can identify which QUIC version both sides agreed to use. The connection IDs are used to associate packets with a QUIC connection independent of the IP address and port, which helps with load balancing and connection migration.

The spin bit is a single bit in the short header that toggles approximately once per round-trip time. This allows passive observers to estimate the latency of QUIC flows without seeing the encrypted packet numbers. Most other packet-level information in QUIC headers is encrypted, including packet numbers, acknowledgments, and control flags.
sections.plainLanguage: QUIC headers come in two sizes. The big one appears during setup and shows the protocol version and connection labels. The small one used during normal data transfer is mostly hidden, except for a bit that blinks to let you measure latency.

sections.title: Network Observations and Management
sections.content:
Network operators can make several observations about QUIC flows on the wire. During the handshake, the pattern of packet exchanges is distinguishable and can indicate that a QUIC connection is being established. The client sends Initial packets containing the TLS ClientHello, the server responds with Initial and Handshake packets, and the client completes the handshake. This observable pattern allows operators to detect connection setup and estimate round-trip time from the handshake delays.

Server Name Indication (SNI), which reveals what server the client is trying to connect to, is visible in the client's Initial packet if it appears in the TLS ClientHello. However, future work on TLS Encrypted Client Hello may hide SNI in the future.

The document also covers practical network management tasks: passive performance measurement (RTT and some congestion signals via ECN), stateful filtering at firewalls and NATs (which need at least a 2-minute timeout even for UDP), QoS handling (which should treat packets of the same QUIC connection uniformly), and path MTU management (where networks should drop oversized packets rather than fragment them and send appropriate ICMP feedback).
sections.plainLanguage: Network tools can watch the handshake to see when a QUIC connection starts, measure the round-trip time using a blink bit, and see which server is being contacted. For managing the network, the key insight is that QUIC makes it impossible to do many things that TCP allows, so operators must ask for the endpoints' cooperation.

sections.title: Management Constraints and Security
sections.content:
QUIC's integrity protection means that no device on the network path can modify the contents of QUIC packets without detection. This is intentional: QUIC encrypts not only application data but also most transport headers. Any modification to a packet causes the integrity check to fail, and the receiver discards it.

This design constraint has significant consequences for network management. Practices that rely on modifying packets in flight—such as changing source or destination addresses, rewriting port numbers, or altering transport-layer flags—cannot work transparently with QUIC. Stateful treatments like NAT rebinding are possible, but they must be done without hiding address changes from the endpoints, because endpoints need to know their actual network addresses to function correctly and defend against amplification attacks.

The document notes that managing QUIC is not one-size-fits-all: what is necessary or mandatory in some networks (like enterprise networks with compliance requirements) may be different from other networks. Network operators should not assume they can use version numbers to reliably identify QUIC traffic, because the protocol is expected to evolve rapidly with many experimental and standard versions deployed simultaneously.
sections.plainLanguage: QUIC is locked up so nobody on the network can mess with it without breaking the connection. This makes some network tricks stop working. Firewalls and load balancers have to cooperate with the endpoints instead of sneaking changes past them.
